newsitem.title: UK: British soccer bribes contacts, cash scrutinised.
newsitem.headline: British soccer bribes contacts, cash scrutinised.

text.p: Four men on trial accused of fixing soccer games for an Asian betting group cannot explain why they handled big cash sums and were in constant contact around match days, prosecutors said.

Chief prosecutor David Calvert Smith, speaking on Thursday at the end of three days in which he outlined his case, said the pattern of non-stop phone calls around match days and large cash sums could only mean one thing.

"Can you draw the inference, as we would like you to do, that the money, telephone calls and matches are linked?" he asked the jury in the southern city of Winchester while discussing the case against Dutch goalkeeper Hans Segers.

Although much media attention has focussed on charismatic former Liverpool goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar, the prosecution only alleges that he tried to fix four matches, and three of those attempts ended in failure.

Former Wimbledon goalkeeper Segers, on the other hand, paid in 104,000 pounds ($175,000) into a Swiss bank account between October 1993 and November 1994, a period which saw his side lose 14 times when he was playing.

Segers and Grobbelaar face separate charges of match-rigging in conjunction with former soccer player John Fashanu and Malaysian businessman Heng Suan Lim, both of whom received large amounts of money from Indonesia.

Neither man could satisfactorily explain where the money came from while Segers' claim that the 104,000 pounds was the proceeds of car thefts carried out when he was much younger was simply ridiculous, the prosecution said.

Calvert Smith said it made more sense to focus on detailed telephone logs and cash payments since it was almost impossible to run through recordings of matches and declare that goalkeepers had deliberately let in certain goals.

"Almost every weekend goals go in where the commentator says 'He should have done better than that'. Of course goals go in which the keeper might have saved, had he had his time again," Calvert Smith told the jury.
"It is impossible to say whether there was a mistake or a deliberate mistake."

On the other hand, the telephone logs and cash payments showed a set pattern of contacts between the keepers and Fashanu and Lim, who almost always called Indonesian numbers just before and after certain games.

In Grobbelaar's case, further evidence was provided by main prosecution witness Chris Vincent, who is due to take the stand next Monday. He covertly recorded Grobbelaar, his former business partner, admitting to rigging games.
Grobbelaar is also accused of accepting 2,000 pounds from Vincent, who claimed to represent a second betting syndicate which wanted games to be thrown.
On one of the covert recordings which Vincent made, Grobbelaar says he received 40,000 pounds in cash for helping Liverpool lose 3-0 at Newcastle in late November 1993. ($1=.5958 Pound)
